checks.goodAnswer: Names at least two independent enforcement layers (application policy check and forced RLS keyed on a transaction-local setting) and shows the tenant ID is derived only from the authenticated session, never from user input. Lists every RLS-bypassing role and why it exists. Points to an automated cross-tenant test suite that runs in CI against a real Postgres with PgBouncer in transaction mode, and to the support-access procedure with its audit trail.
checks.label: Tenant isolation
probes: Where does the tenant ID used for the decision come from (session claim, subdomain, URL, request body), and can a user influence it?
Is the application check backed by Postgres Row-Level Security with FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, so that a missing `where tenant_id = ...` still returns no rows?
Is the tenant set with SET LOCAL inside each transaction by the Prisma extension, and what proves it cannot leak to the next transaction on the same PgBouncer connection?
Which database roles bypass RLS (table owner, migration role, BYPASSRLS), which services use them, and how is their use restricted and logged?
Do Temporal workflows, BullMQ jobs, caches (Redis keys), search indexes and object-storage paths carry and enforce the tenant ID, or do they trust the caller?
Can a user who belongs to two tenants (for example counsel appearing before two institutions) ever have permissions or data from one tenant applied in the other?
How is Nomology staff or support access to a tenant granted: tenant consent, time limit, scope, and audit entry visible to the tenant?
checks.question: Can any rule, code path or operator action in this control grant access to another tenant's data, and what independent layers stop it if one layer fails?
redFlags: Tenant isolation relies only on application code or on developers remembering a filter
Tenant ID read from a header, query string or request body without checking it against the session
Background jobs or workflows run with a superuser or BYPASSRLS role by default
No test that tries to read, write or enumerate another tenant's records

checks.goodAnswer: Provides a complete inventory of entry points mapped to the enforcement function each one calls, and names the mechanism that makes deny the default for anything not mapped. States the maximum lifetime of any token or link that outlives a permission change (for example pre-signed URLs at 5 minutes or less) and explains how derived data such as search results and AI context is filtered by the same policy.
checks.label: Enforcement points and bypass paths
probes: List every entry point that touches the asset: Next.js route handlers, server actions, server components, public APIs, webhooks, Temporal signal and activity handlers, BullMQ jobs, exports, admin tools, and database consoles.
Is the check centralised in one shared package in the monorepo that all of these call, and how is a new route prevented from shipping without it (lint rule, middleware default-deny, CI check)?
Are file downloads (pre-signed URLs, transcripts, eBundles) checked at issue time, and how long do the links stay valid after access is revoked?
Do derived copies of the data (search index, AI embeddings or prompts, notification emails, cached PDFs, analytics extracts) inherit the same access rules?
Is authorisation checked on the server for every request, rather than relying on hidden buttons or client-side state?
For long-running workflows, is the permission re-checked when the action executes, not only when the workflow started days earlier?
checks.question: Is this control enforced on every path that reaches the protected asset, including non-interactive and indirect paths, with no way around it?
redFlags: Checks performed only in the UI or only in some API routes
Workflows or jobs act on stale permissions captured at start time
Long-lived download links, or search and AI features that bypass the policy
No mechanism that fails the build when a new route lacks an authorisation call

checks.goodAnswer: Gives a numeric revocation target and the mechanism that meets it, names the scheduled job that expires time-bound grants with a monitored failure alert, and describes break-glass access with approval, a hard time limit and tenant-visible audit. Shows that role and policy changes are themselves permissioned, logged and, for sensitive roles, approved by a second person.
checks.label: Grant lifecycle and privileged access
probes: How quickly does revocation take effect across active sessions, caches and open WebSocket or streaming connections (target in seconds or minutes)?
Which grants are time-bound (transcriber per hearing, temporary co-counsel, interpreter), and what job expires them and alerts if expiry fails?
What happens to a user's access when they leave a law firm, are removed from a case, or when an arbitrator is challenged or recused?
How are conflicts and ethical walls applied when a user is added to a case, and can a tenant admin override them?
Is there a break-glass process for platform staff, with approval, time limit, session recording and post-use review?
Who can change roles or policies, is it maker-checker for high-impact changes, and are tenant admins prevented from granting themselves tribunal-only access?
With SSO (SAML or OIDC), how are de-provisioned identity-provider accounts reflected (SCIM, session lifetime, re-check on token refresh)?
checks.question: How are permissions granted, changed, expired and revoked, and how is privileged or emergency access controlled?
redFlags: Revocation only takes effect at next login or after a long session timeout
Standing (permanent) platform-admin access to tenant data
Time-bound grants with no automated expiry
Tenant admins able to escalate themselves into tribunal-only or party-restricted data

refs.title: NIST SP 800-63B Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management

checks.goodAnswer: States fail-closed behaviour for each dependency with the user-facing message, gives cache lifetimes and the invalidation trigger, and names the key store, key owner and rotation interval per region. Includes a tested rotation runbook with a recorded rehearsal date and a latency budget for the check.
checks.label: Failure modes and secrets
probes: If the policy store, identity provider, Redis or KMS is unavailable or slow, does the request get denied, and what does the user see?
Are policy decisions cached; if so, for how long, and how are caches invalidated when a role or policy changes?
Where are signing keys, encryption keys and client secrets held (AWS KMS / Azure Key Vault, per region), who can use them, and what is the rotation period?
What is the procedure and expected time to rotate a compromised key or secret without downtime, and has it been rehearsed?
What added latency does the check introduce at p95 and p99, and what stops teams from bypassing it for performance?
Are rate limits and lockouts tuned so that they block brute force and enumeration without letting an attacker lock out a tribunal before a hearing?
checks.question: What does the control do when its dependencies fail or its keys and secrets are compromised, and does it always fail closed?
redFlags: Any path that allows access when the policy engine or identity provider errors
Secrets in environment files, source code or CI logs
No tested key rotation procedure
Unbounded policy caches with no invalidation on change

checks.goodAnswer: Gives a table of each data element the control touches with its storage location per region and per cloud, and identifies any cross-border flow with its legal basis and sub-processor entry. Shows how parity between AWS and Azure deployments is checked.
checks.label: Data residency
probes: Are session stores, audit logs, key material and policy data deployed per region (India, Singapore, US), or is any of it global?
Does a global component (login page, identity provider, CDN, email or SMS provider, error tracking) receive personal data or tokens of tenants pinned to another region?
How does a user who works with tenants in two regions sign in, and where is their identity record stored?
Do security logs shipped to a SIEM or monitoring vendor leave the region, and is that covered by the sub-processor list and transfer terms?
Where a client requires Azure, is the control implemented identically there, and how is parity verified?
checks.question: Does every piece of data this control creates or uses (sessions, audit logs, keys, identity data) stay in the tenant's pinned region?
redFlags: A single global session or audit store for all regions
Personal data in logs sent to a vendor outside the tenant's region without a recorded transfer basis
Azure deployments assumed to match AWS without verification

checks.goodAnswer: Lists the logged event types with their fields, names the storage and the tamper-evidence mechanism, and states retention per region with the legal or contractual basis for each period. Explains how a tenant retrieves its own trail and how log access is itself logged.
checks.label: Audit trail
probes: Which events are logged: logins, MFA changes, role grants and removals, policy changes, denials, reads of highly confidential items such as award drafts, exports and break-glass use?
Does each event carry tenant ID, actor, acting-on-behalf-of, resource ID, action, decision, reason code, policy version, source IP, request ID and UTC timestamp?
How is the log protected from change or deletion, including by platform administrators (append-only table, write-once storage, hash chaining)?
How long are logs kept, and does this meet CERT-In (logs kept for 180 days within India), DPDP Rules and tenant contract requirements?
Can a tenant admin or tribunal export the audit trail for their own cases without seeing other tenants' events?
Are personal data and secrets kept out of log messages, or masked?
checks.question: Are grants, denials, privilege changes and sensitive reads recorded in a tamper-evident log that can answer who did what, when, to which record, and under which policy version?
redFlags: Denials or reads of sensitive documents not logged
Audit records stored in a table the application can update or delete
Retention period not stated or shorter than CERT-In's 180 days for India-region systems
Passwords, tokens or full document contents written to logs

refs.title: CERT-In Directions under section 70B(6) of the IT Act, 28 April 2022
NIST SP 800-92 Guide to Computer Security Log Management

checks.goodAnswer: Names each detection rule with its threshold, destination and on-call owner, and links each to a runbook. Shows the hand-off from alert to incident to regulatory notification with the clock start defined, so that the 6-hour CERT-In and 72-hour DPDP and GDPR deadlines can be met.
checks.label: Detection and alerting
probes: Which patterns are alerted on: denial spikes per user or tenant, sequential ID probing, cross-tenant access attempts, impossible travel, mass downloads, privilege escalation, break-glass use?
What are the thresholds and how were they chosen to avoid both silence and alert fatigue?
Who receives alerts out of hours, what is the response time target, and where is the runbook?

How does a confirmed incident trigger notification clocks: CERT-In within 6 hours, the Data Protection Board and affected people under DPDP (detailed report within 72 hours), GDPR supervisory authority within 72 hours, and Singapore PDPC within 3 days of assessing a notifiable breach?
Are tenants told about security events affecting their cases, and within what contractual timeframe?
Is there a dashboard of denials and anomalies per tenant that the security team reviews on a fixed cadence?
checks.question: Which signals from this control are monitored, what thresholds raise an alert, who responds, and how does an alert feed the incident and breach-notification process?
redFlags: Denials logged but nobody alerted
No named on-call responder or runbook
No link between security alerts and the breach-notification procedure

refs.title: PDPC Guide on Managing and Notifying Data Breaches under the PDPA

checks.goodAnswer: Gives a table of clause IDs per framework mapped to the specific requirement IDs in this spec, with links to the compliance control nodes that operate and evidence them. Calls out any contractual requirement that goes beyond the frameworks.
checks.label: Framework and legal mapping
probes: Which ISO 27001:2022 Annex A controls apply (for example 5.15 access control, 5.18 access rights, 8.2 privileged access, 8.3 information access restriction, 8.5 secure authentication, 8.15 logging, 8.24 use of cryptography)?
Which SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria apply (for example CC6.1 to CC6.3 logical access, CC7.2 monitoring), and which compliance control nodes reference this spec?
Which privacy duties does it support: DPDP reasonable security safeguards and access controls, GDPR Article 32 security of processing, PDPA protection obligation?
Do HKIAC, SEBI ODR or other client contracts impose specific requirements (MFA for all users, IP allow-listing, data segregation, audit rights)?
What evidence does the control produce automatically for audits (access review exports, configuration snapshots, test results)?
If ISO 42001 applies (AI features use this data), how are AI components covered?
checks.question: Which specific clauses of ISO 27001:2022, SOC 2, privacy laws and client contracts does this control help satisfy, and what evidence will an auditor take from it?
redFlags: Generic statements such as 'supports ISO 27001' with no clause IDs
No link to the compliance control that operates and evidences this mechanism
Client contractual security requirements not checked

refs.title: AICPA 2017 Trust Services Criteria (with revised points of focus, 2022)
Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 (Gazette notification)

checks.goodAnswer: Shows a test suite derived from the matrix with a coverage report per row, run in CI on every change to policies or routes. States pen-test frequency (at least annually and after major changes), scope including cross-tenant and IDOR testing, and fix deadlines by severity (for example critical within 7 days).
checks.label: Verification and testing
probes: Is there at least one automated negative test per matrix row and condition (wrong role, wrong case stage, expired assignment, other party, other tenant)?
Are the tests generated from the matrix itself, so a change to the matrix without a matching test fails CI?
Do tests run against a real Postgres with RLS and PgBouncer in transaction mode, not a mock?
Do tests cover Temporal handlers, BullMQ jobs and export paths, not only HTTP routes?
What is the scope, frequency and provider of penetration testing, does it include multi-tenant and authorisation abuse cases, and how fast are findings fixed by severity?
Is there a regression test for every past access-control bug or pen-test finding?
checks.question: How is every allow and deny in the permission matrix proven by automated tests, and what independent testing covers what automation cannot?
redFlags: Only positive (happy-path) tests
Tests run with RLS disabled or against mocked authorisation
No pen test, or a pen test scoped without authorisation and tenant isolation testing
No fix deadlines for findings

refs.title: OWASP Authorization Testing Automation Cheat Sheet

depth: 4–10 pages. The permission matrix and threat table must be complete for the scope; partial matrices are the main source of access bugs. Map each requirement to an OWASP ASVS 5.0 requirement ID where one exists, and always state the ASVS version (chapter numbers changed between 4.0.3 and 5.0). Split by persona or resource family if the matrix exceeds ~40 rows.
name: Access and security control
purpose: Specifies a mechanism that decides who can do what, or protects data and sessions, with its threats and verification made explicit.

sections.example: Case-level authorization decides whether a user may view or act on a case, its documents and hearings. Every API route and Temporal signal handler that touches case data calls it.
sections.guide: What is protected, from whom, and which parts of the platform rely on this control.
sections.label: Purpose and scope

sections.example:
| Asset | Classification |
|---|---|
| Pleadings and evidence documents | Confidential — party-restricted |
| Award drafts | Highly confidential — tribunal only |
| Party contact details | Personal data (DPDP / GDPR) |
sections.guide: The data and actions being protected, with sensitivity classification.
sections.label: Protected assets

sections.example:
| Role | Acquired by |
|---|---|
| Claimant / respondent counsel | Invitation accepted on the case |
| Neutral (arbitrator) | Appointment accepted |
| Tribunal secretary | Tenant admin assignment |
| Tenant admin | Platform onboarding |
| Transcriber | Assigned per hearing, expires after delivery |
sections.guide: Every persona and system actor, and how a user acquires each role.
sections.label: Actors and roles

sections.example:
| Resource / action | Counsel | Neutral | Secretary | Transcriber |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| View own party's filings | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | — |
| View other party's filings | after service | ✓ | ✓ | — |
| View award draft | — | ✓ | — | — |
| Upload transcript | — | — | ✓ | assigned hearing only |
sections.guide: Role × resource × action, including conditions (case stage, ownership). Use a table; every cell must be decided.
sections.label: Permission matrix

sections.example: RBAC for coarse roles, ABAC conditions on `case.stage`, `document.visibility` and `assignment.expiresAt`. Policies are versioned data in the Rules engine; evaluation is deny-by-default and returns a reason code.
sections.guide: How rules are expressed and evaluated (RBAC, ABAC attributes, policy engine), where policies live, and evaluation order.
sections.label: Policy model

sections.example:
| STRIDE | Scenario | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Elevation | Counsel edits case ID in URL to another case | Case membership check on every request + RLS |
| Information disclosure | Transcriber keeps access after delivery | Time-bound assignment, nightly expiry job |
| Repudiation | Neutral denies viewing a document | Read events in audit trail |
sections.guide: STRIDE-style table: threat, scenario, mitigation, residual risk.
sections.label: Threats and abuse cases

sections.example: Return 404 (not 403) for resources in cases the user is not a member of. Log denial with reason code and policy version. Show "You don't have access to this document" only within a case the user belongs to.
sections.guide: What the user sees on denial, what is logged, and how errors avoid leaking existence of resources.
sections.label: Denial behaviour

sections.example:
- SEC-AZ-1 Access control is enforced server-side on every request (ASVS 5.0 V8 Authorization)
- SEC-AZ-2 Deny by default; new resources are inaccessible until a rule grants access
- SEC-AZ-3 Privilege changes take effect within 60 seconds across all sessions
sections.guide: Numbered, testable requirements, each mapped to an ASVS item where possible.
sections.label: Security requirements

sections.example: Matrix-driven test suite: one allowed and one denied test per matrix row, generated from the matrix itself. Annual external pen test covers IDOR on case and document routes.
sections.guide: Automated negative tests, review steps, pen-test scope.
sections.label: Verification
